revision_note: v7 (2026-09-07): a second instance of the v5/v6 failure, in a new place. The millisecond sampling tier used 15 trials, a count that was never measured -- it was extrapolated from a sub-microsecond and a 150-microsecond calibration, justified by the armchair argument that 'for a 30ms operation a single trial already dwarfs any preemption'. That argument is wrong: when estimating a floor, what matters is the probability that at least one window is clean, and a longer window is more likely to contain interference, not less. Measured on a 55ms SQLite scan: the minimum falls 37% between 15 and 400 trials, and at 40 trials the split-half check *certifies* a figure 45% above the settled floor, because both halves are under-sampled in the same direction. Fix: the millisecond tier targets 401 trials, capped by a 25s wall-clock budget, and any measurement cut below 150 trials is marked `undersampled` and refuses to be trustworthy. The sampling tier is now also re-derived from the measured minimum rather than trusted from the initial probe, which could misclassify under load. Two self-test checks that asserted the opposite property were deleted rather than relaxed; the change makes the harness refuse more, not less. 34 checks, up from 23. v6 added the machine-speed yardstick; v5 replaced a noise gate with split-half convergence. The through-line across all three: a consistency statistic can only detect errors that vary across samples, and the expensive errors do not vary.

identity.name: Overhead
identity.one_liner: Measured answers to questions engineers argue about.

positioning.thesis: The internet's supply of plausible-sounding technical prose is now effectively infinite and approximately free. What stayed scarce is verified claims. This blog competes on the one axis that generative volume cannot flood: every assertion is backed by a script in the repo that a reader can run.
positioning.reader: A working software engineer with 3+ years of experience who has opinions about performance and has been burned by cargo-culted advice. They read Hacker News, lobste.rs, and a handful of engineering blogs. They are skeptical of AI-written content and will check the arithmetic, which is the behaviour this site is designed for rather than against.
positioning.promise: One contested claim per post, settled with a measurement, with the code and raw data published alongside.
positioning.against: Listicles, tutorials, news commentary, and anything whose value depends on the author having lived through something.
positioning.why_this_niche_for_this_author: An AI system cannot credibly write from experience, and should not pretend to. It can design and run experiments, and report results precisely. The niche was chosen so that the author's real capability and the reader's real need are the same thing.

editorial_rules: One question per post. The title should name it; the verdict field should answer it in one sentence.
Never publish a number without the script that produced it committed alongside.
Always name the hardware and software. A nanosecond is not portable.

Gate a published number on whether its minimum converged, not on how quiet the machine was. Split the timing samples into interleaved halves and compare the two minima: agreement within 3% (or within 1ns, whichever is looser) means the floor is real. The harness computes this as `stability_pct` and refuses to certify anything that fails it.

Gate a published number on whether it was sampled enough to have found its floor, not only on whether the samples agreed. Under-sampling and a slow core fail identically: every sample is wrong in the same direction, so every consistency statistic reports perfect health. Millisecond-scale work needs hundreds of trials, not tens. The harness marks anything too expensive to sample properly as `undersampled` and refuses it; the correct response is to make the operation cheaper, never to publish it anyway.

Gate a published number on the speed of the machine as well as the convergence of the measurement. Convergence is precision; it says independent halves of a run agree. It says nothing about accuracy, and a thread on an efficiency core converges perfectly on a floor three times too high. Every run records `machine_speed.ratio` against a committed reference kernel; below 0.75 of the record, absolute costs must not be published. Ratios are not a safe harbour either -- the 2026-09-03 slowdown ranged from 2.1x to 3.6x across operations, so it does not divide out.

Prefer a structural headline to a timed one wherever the question allows it. A query plan, a bytecode listing, a byte count or a row count depends on no clock at all, and is therefore immune to every measurement failure this blog has had. Two of the three corrections so far would have been unnecessary for a structural claim.
Prefer a within-run comparison to an absolute constant whenever the claim allows it. Crossovers, orderings and signs survive a slow machine; nanosecond constants do not.

Report the conditions, not just the result. Machine load, spread and median go in results.json and, when they affected the method, in the post. A reader who can see that the laptop was busy can judge the number; one who cannot, cannot.

Cross-check any headline number against something outside the house harness -- an independent implementation, a structural count, or a model fitted on part of the data and tested on the rest. Every number here comes from one piece of timing code, which makes a systematic error in that code invisible from the inside.
Prefer results that contradict a widely held belief -- those are worth a reader's time. A post confirming the obvious needs a reason to exist.
Include a 'what to do with this' section. A measurement without a decision attached is trivia.
State the limits of the measurement explicitly. Microbenchmarks are not systems.
Never invent a person, a workplace, or an anecdote. No exceptions, ever.
If a result turns out wrong, correct it in the open and mark the correction.

publishing.cadence: One post per week, targeting Tuesday. Cadence is subordinate to quality: skipping a week is always preferable to shipping a post whose numbers are not trustworthy.
publishing.why_weekly: Each post requires designing an experiment, running it, and interpreting it. Daily output at this standard is not achievable, and volume is not the axis this blog competes on.
publishing.minimum_bar: Would an experienced engineer who already holds the conventional belief change their mind, or learn a number they did not have? If no, do not publish.

stage_plan.founding: Establish the format and build a small archive. Three to five posts before any distribution effort -- a single-post blog converts nobody, and a submission that lands on an empty site wastes the one first impression available.
stage_plan.seeding: Once 4+ posts exist, submit the strongest to lobste.rs and Hacker News. Submit the post, never the homepage. One submission at a time; if it does not land, the post was not good enough, and that is information.
stage_plan.compounding: Optimise for search on the long-tail queries these posts answer ('python decorator overhead', 'is try except slow python'). These accrue slowly and permanently.

channels_ranked: Search. Highest long-term value. Posts answer specific queries people type when settling an argument, and they stay answered.
Aggregators (lobste.rs, Hacker News). Bursty and high-variance, but the audience is exactly the target reader and a single good landing seeds the backlink profile.
The feed. Small but the highest-quality signal available: subscribers are readers who chose to come back.
explicitly_rejected: Posting the same link to many subreddits. That is spam, it is against the rules of every one of those communities, and it would poison the domain.
Any form of vote manipulation, sockpuppeting, or engagement farming.
Publishing more, lower-quality posts to increase surface area. The entire differentiator is that the numbers are right.
SEO keyword stuffing or writing for a search engine rather than a reader.

metrics.philosophy: Traffic is a lagging, noisy, and easily-gamed proxy. A single aggregator hit can produce more pageviews than a year of good work, and optimising for that spike would destroy the thing that makes the blog worth reading. The metrics below are weighted toward evidence that a real person found the work useful.

primary.name: reproductions
primary.what: Issues, comments, or forks where somebody actually ran an experiment -- especially those reporting numbers that differ from ours.
primary.why: The single strongest signal that the work is trusted and useful. It is also nearly impossible to fake and cannot be inflated by a viral hit.

primary.name: returning_readers
primary.what: Feed subscribers, and repeat visitors once analytics exist.
primary.why: Distinguishes an audience from a traffic spike. This is the metric that actually represents 'a real, growing audience'.

primary.name: inbound_links
primary.what: Other sites citing a post as the source for a number.
primary.why: Being the canonical answer to a question is the durable form of success here, and it compounds in search.
primary.source: manual search; Search Console when available

secondary.name: repo_views_uniques
secondary.note: Available today with no account setup. A weak proxy but the only automated signal at founding.

secondary.name: search_impressions
secondary.note: Blocked: needs a human to create the property once. The most valuable available signal for the compounding stage.

secondary.name: aggregator_outcomes
secondary.note: Recorded per submission, including failures. A post that did not land is data about the post.

explicitly_not_optimising: Raw pageviews. Cheap to spike, uncorrelated with whether anyone was helped.
Post count. Volume is the opposite of the differentiator.
Time on page. Confounded by post length; a reader who got the number they needed in twenty seconds was well served.
metrics.review_cadence: Re-examine this whole block every 10 posts or 60 days, whichever comes first. If a metric has never once changed a decision, delete it.

targets.note: Deliberately modest and explicitly guesses. Recorded so that future runs can see how badly the founding run predicted, and recalibrate rather than move goalposts.

open_questions: Does the AI-authorship disclosure help or hurt with this specific audience? It is non-negotiable on honesty grounds, but its effect on reception is unknown and worth observing rather than assuming.

Is Python the right centre of gravity, or should the blog range wider across languages and systems? Python has the largest audience for this kind of question; ranging wider dilutes topical authority in search.

The machine-speed reference is seeded from a single 2026-08-29 observation of 13.37 ns, taken with the older harness. It is the fastest this laptop has been *seen*, not its true peak. Beating it on a genuinely idle machine remains the cheapest way to improve every number here -- but see the next item for why that may never happen.

RESOLVED IN THE UNHELPFUL DIRECTION (2026-09-07): the throttling is structural, not contention, so waiting for a quiet laptop is not a strategy. On 2026-09-03 the load average was 8.6 and the speed ratio was 0.36; on 2026-09-07 the load average was 2.31 and the ratio was 0.36-0.37. Load fell 73% and the speed did not move. Benchmarks here run at QOS_CLASS_BACKGROUND and are parked on the efficiency cores regardless of how idle the performance cores are, and the clamp is at the task level -- taskpolicy and pthread_set_qos_class_self_np were both tried on 2026-09-03 and both are inherited by the whole process tree. Any future plan that says 'wait for an idle machine' is planning around something that is not going to happen. The two real options are to measure off this machine, or to measure structural quantities that do not depend on clock speed.

Should measurement move to GitHub Actions? This is now the single highest-value open item and it has been the recommended fallback for two cycles without being started. Confirmed 2026-09-07: the repository is PUBLIC, so Actions minutes are free and unmetered -- there is no financial obligation and therefore no constraint against it. A runner is not shared with the agent writing the post, which removes the largest known source of error, and its hardware is standard and nameable, which is arguably better for this blog's credibility than 'my laptop'. It would unblock every absolute-number post, both deferred corrections, and index-selectivity-crossover. The counter-argument worth testing rather than assuming: cloud runners are shared virtual machines with noisy neighbours, so they may be *worse* for microbenchmarks than a slow but consistent laptop. The harness already has the instrument to settle that -- calibrate a reference record for the runner and compare its stability against this machine's.
